Manhwa Review: Absolute Regression

Listen to audio version of this article
Sponsored by
0:00 / 4:50
Instaread

If you’ve spent any time in the manhwa world (or heck, if you’ve watch any “turn back the clock” anime like Re:Zero), the premise to Absolute Regression is going to sound pretty typical; but hear me out. Mugeok is an old Murim (martial arts) warrior whose “cult” (clan) was wiped out decades earlier by an overwhelmingly powerful foe, the mysterious Mugi. Since then, Mugeok has been on a quest to gather several legendary artifacts that together will allow him to travel back to the past and prepare for the attack. His ultimate goal? To find and kill Mugi. The ritual succeeds, Mugeok returns to when he was a young man, and with his future knowledge has a secret advantage over the foes and obstacles awaiting him.

So far, not too much to write home about, right?

But what might sound like a typical regression/revenge cultivation fantasy quickly proves to be something far deeper. When the man overseeing the time-travel ritual succeeds in creating the portal, he tries to send himself through it instead of Mugeok. Our main character sees everything he has been seeking for decades about to be lost, and comes close to killing the other man; only at the last minute does he forgive him and turn to go through the portal.

And then…time stops. A divine being appears and announces that the real conditions for the ritual were not the treasures that Mugeok has spent his life finding, but the sacrifices he made along the way—and the final sacrifice was forgiving the man who just tried to betray him.

Forgiveness, in a quest for revenge? Yes, here we find one of the central tensions and themes of Absolute Regression. What will Mugeok do now, as he sets out to correct the past with the message of forgiveness ringing in his ears? And indeed, as Mugeok undertakes his new journey, he often finds himself second-guessing his initial impressions of others, uncovering the deeper layers of their humanity where previously he had brushed them off after jumping to superficial judgments.

In this respect, there may be a little Mugeok in all of us.

Alongside such themes, the foremost strength of this series is, more than anything else, its complex characters and the powerful interpersonal dynamics it weaves between them. The first step Mugeok takes after regressing is to seek to mend and deepen his relationship with his cold and harsh father; and their slowly healing connection becomes a recurring motif through the story. Then there is An, Mugeok’s bodyguard: It’s a common trope in manhwa (and visual media of all stripes) to depict the central women of the cast as very thin, and rare for them to be heavyset or obese. But An demonstrates that likeable, beautiful female characters don’t have to be portrayed according to the fantastically thin and curvy stereotype (and she has even become a fan favorite, judging by the comments on Webtoons.com).

There are many other excellent examples of nuanced characters and relationships, but the best so far probably consists of the interactions between two deuteragonists, Paso and the Shackled Man. Their arc (which begins around chapter 65 or so) reads like an extended, haunting, and painfully beautiful version of the gospel parable of the Pearl of Great Price. It becomes increasingly clear that Paso will have to face a choice: Will he join hands with Mugeok, at the cost of all of his great treasures and his very position of power at the top of his sect (faction), or will he refuse to part with the old life he knows and the comforts at his beck and call?

As I read these chapters, I couldn’t help feeling time and time again that there is a Paso in all of us.

The themes and characters alone would be worth the price of admittance. But to top it all off, we also have artist Park Jin Hwan’s gorgeous, stunning artwork: Worth mentioning in particular are the sublime landscapes created in the traditional Chinese style, which yet somehow blend seamlessly with the manhwa-style characters to create a harmony worthy of the epic story being told. The same might be said of the numerous lengthy and detailed spreads: individual scenes spread out over so many screens that you will find yourself scrolling and thinking, “When is this single panel going to end? Not that I mind, though—it’s a visual feast.”

I have read dozens, if not hundreds, of webtoons in my day, but rarely have I found one that is so high-quality by every benchmark. If the frequent violence (bloody, but not generally gory, and to be expected given the themes and genre) does not put you off, then this story is a treasure you won’t want to miss.

Absolute Regression is published on Webtoon.

Written by negativeprimes

Dr. Steve, aka NegativePrimes, was introduced to anime while working on his Ph.D. in literary studies, when the local anime club showed Naruto’s fight against Zabuza and Haku on an auditorium big screen. His favorite anime series include FMA: Brotherhood, Erased, Snow White with Red Hair, and Gate, and he also enjoys computer programming, gaming, and technology. Where he finds the time for these, after prayer, work, and raising several children, remains something of a mystery.
